title: Most Germans Want Minimum Age for Social Media
author: Katharina Wedel, Larissa Zierow, and colleagues
summary: The ifo Education Survey finds that 85% of German adults and 47% of adolescents themselves support a minimum age of 16 for social media, providing the first large-n evidence that pressure for such a law is not top-down moral panic but intergenerational consensus. The finding matters because it shifts the permission structure for policy: when adolescents say they would welcome a delay, the standard objection that age limits are paternalistic loses its force. Educators face two takeaways. First, the political window for phone-free schools and social-media age limits is open in more places than English-speaking press notices; Germany is a data point in a broader international wave. Second, the fact that adolescents themselves are on board changes the classroom conversation from adults-against-kids to one where many students already agree the current arrangement is harmful.
points: Nearly half of German adolescents themselves support a minimum age of 16 for social media, transforming the policy argument from paternalism to evidence of intergenerational consensus.
Germany's 85% adult support and 47% adolescent support show the political window for phone-free schools and social-media age limits is open in multiple countries simultaneously.
In the classroom, adolescent support for limits changes the conversation from adults-against-kids to a discussion where many students already recognise the current arrangement as harmful to them.
quotes: An overwhelming majority of German adults — 85 percent — support a minimum age of 16 years for using social media. This is the finding of the latest ifo Education Survey.

What is perhaps even more striking is that 47 percent of adolescents themselves support a minimum age of 16 for social media use. Nearly half of the population that would be affected by such a rule says, in effect, “yes, we would welcome this.

These results land in a specific policy moment. Germany is debating whether to follow Australia’s lead in setting a legal minimum age for social media, and this survey provides the clearest evidence yet of broad public support for such a move.” “The survey adds to the growing cross-national case that adolescent social media saturation is not a narrow mental health problem but a developmental problem, and that policy tools of the kind Australia has pioneered have much wider public backing than the debate often assumes.

When nearly half of adolescents themselves say they would welcome a delay in access, the standard objection that age limits are paternalistic becomes much harder to sustain. Teens, not just parents, are telling the survey they see the harm.

The political window for a phone-free childhood, longer than many policymakers have assumed, is open. What the survey shows is that the public, and crucially a large share of the affected age group, is ready.

These findings should sharpen the case for action. Germany, like Australia, can move from debate to legislation, and it can do so knowing that the evidence of public support is no longer thin or speculative.

Delaying social media access until 16 is not just a parental preference. It is a position a near-majority of adolescents themselves endorse, and an overwhelming majority of adults share.” Archived from After Babel (Jonathan Haidt newsletter) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
